moves.sectionTitle: Modal Possibility and Contingent Explanation
moves.currentDescription: Because maximal greatness includes omnipotence, omniscience, and goodness in every possible world, God's possible existence entails necessary existence and thus existence in the actual world.
moves.lockedProposition: The possibility of a maximally great being entails its necessary and therefore actual existence.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: that implies is that if God's existence is even possible then God must exist for if a maximally great being exists in some possible world he exists in all of them that's part of what it means to be maximally great to be all powerful all knowing and all good in every logically possible world so if God's existence is even possible then he exists in every logically possible world and therefore in the actual world we can summarize this argument as follows premise one it's possible that a maximally great being God exists two if it's possible that a maximally great being exist exists then a maximally great being
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The move defines maximal greatness across every logically possible world, then connects possible instantiation, necessary existence, and actuality, giving the modal inference clarity and relevance to God's existence. Principal limitation: The excerpt supports the conditional by unpacking maximal greatness, but does not independently establish the possibility premise, leaving evidential warrant and calibration materially weaker than logical presentation, precision, and responsiveness. Live burden: Pro must justify that a maximally great being is logically possible, rather than merely conceivable or definitionally stipulated, and show that omnipotence, omniscience, and perfect goodness can be jointly instantiated.

moves.sectionTitle: Modal Possibility and Contingent Explanation
moves.currentDescription: Stenger compares defining God into existence with positing the greatest possible pizza, arguing logic cannot establish existence unless its disputed premises independently warrant it.
moves.lockedProposition: The ontological inference resembles other definition-driven existence claims, and logic alone adds nothing beyond disputable premises.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Stenger directly challenges ontological possibility entailment through the greatest possible pizza comparison, demanding justification for definitions producing actual existence for God but not comparably stipulated objects. Principal limitation: The comparison never analyzes modal possibility, necessary existence, or differences between maximal greatness and pizza quality, leaving an illustrative counterexample without the developed warrant required to establish equivalent reasoning. Live burden: The objection must demonstrate that possibility is definition driven or isolate an invalid inferential step, while explaining why necessary existence cannot distinguish God from the pizza stipulation.

moves.sectionTitle: Modal Possibility and Contingent Explanation
moves.currentDescription: The universe encompasses all spacetime, so its contingent existence requires an explanation beyond physical spacetime, inferred to be a transcendent personal cause.
moves.lockedProposition: Because the universe exists contingently, its explanation must be an external, transcendent personal cause.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Grounding the argument in the universe as all spacetime yields an inference that its contingent explanation must be external, transcendent, and nonphysical, directly supporting a divine cause. Principal limitation: Transcendence follows from locating the explanation beyond space and time, but neither the universe's contingency nor the transition from nonphysical to personal is established, weakening evidence warrant and calibration. Live burden: Pro must defend contingency and demonstrate why the required external explanation entails agency, while excluding impersonal transcendent alternatives capable of explaining spacetime without personhood.

moves.sectionTitle: Modal Possibility and Contingent Explanation
moves.currentDescription: Nothingness needs no explanation because it contains nothing to explain; however, that comparison leaves contingent reality's alleged necessity and personal cause requiring independent support.
moves.lockedProposition: Nothing needs no explanation because nothing exists to explain, whereas contingent reality points to a necessary personal cause.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The reply supplies a comprehensible conceptual reason that nothingness requires no explanation, because no entity or fact exists to be explained, directly confronting the default-nothingness challenge. Principal limitation: This coherent observation cannot establish that contingent reality terminates in a necessary cause, especially a transcendent personal cause, while the natural zero-energy model and alternative accounts remain substantially unanswered. Live burden: Craig must justify the transition from cosmic contingency to necessity and personality, while demonstrating why zero-energy cosmology neither satisfies nor dissolves the demand for external explanation.

moves.sectionTitle: Modal Possibility and Contingent Explanation
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues that the pizza parody lacks coherence, while genuine possibility of maximal greatness entails the ontological conclusion, leaving possibility as the key burden.
moves.lockedProposition: The pizza parody is incoherent, whereas if maximal greatness is genuinely possible the ontological conclusion follows.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The move confronts the pizza analogy by distinguishing an incoherent parody from maximal greatness and identifies genuine possibility as the precondition that carries the ontological conclusion. Principal limitation: The warrant is compressed because it asserts the pizza's incoherence without displaying the contradiction, and it does not establish that maximal greatness is possible, matching the evidence support and charitable comparison. Live burden: The reply must specify why the pizza concept cannot be maximized while maximal greatness can, then defend that possibility rather than letting the parody objection relocate the dispute.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
moves.currentDescription: Because the universe began, Craig argues it cannot arise uncaused from nothing, so its origin requires a timeless, spaceless, immaterial, immensely powerful personal creator.
moves.lockedProposition: Whatever begins has a cause; the universe began, so a timeless, spaceless, powerful personal creator caused it.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig syllogistically connects the universe's beginning and beginning's causal rule to a transcendent cause, then derives timelessness, spacelessness, immateriality, and immense power from causing space and time. Principal limitation: The excerpt asserts both premises without substantiating cosmic beginning or demonstrating causation governs the boundary where time originates, and the further step from a transcendent cause to a personal creator remains undefended. Live burden: Craig must establish the relevant beginning, justify applying the causal premise beyond spacetime, and explain why the cause is a personal being rather than another timeless explanatory condition.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues satellite measurements put cosmic energy density at critical density, consistent with an initial zero-energy state, so cosmic formation requires no divine energy input.
moves.lockedProposition: A zero-energy expanding cosmos can form order without a miracle and at most leaves an inactive deistic creator.

Principal limitation: Critical-density agreement is compatible with zero total energy, yet the excerpt presents compatibility as confirmation, neglects rival cosmological interpretations, and overextends physical sufficiency into an inactive-deity conclusion. Live burden: He must establish why measured density confirms the proposed initial state, explain how zero net energy produces ordered expansion, and exclude active divine causation rather than merely remove an energy-source puzzle.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues that balanced positive matter and negative gravitational energy still describe physical reality, while a quantum vacuum is not nothing, so causation remains required.
moves.lockedProposition: Zero net cosmic energy does not remove the need for a cause, and the quantum vacuum is structured physical reality rather than nothing.

Live burden: The reply must establish why zero aggregate energy still requires an external cause, and why tunneling presupposes sufficiently structured physical conditions to leave origin unexplained.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
moves.currentDescription: Peer-reviewed cosmological models derive quantum tunneling from established physics, making a natural cosmic origin possible and challenging any claim that divine causation is necessary.
moves.lockedProposition: Published quantum-tunneling scenarios show that a natural cosmic origin is consistent with known physics without invoking God.

Live burden: The move must show the tunneling account reaches cosmic origin rather than relocating it, and that consistency with known physics warrants rejecting necessary divine causation rather than permitting a natural alternative.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
moves.currentDescription: Because quantum equations admit deterministic interpretations and vacuum events arise from physical states, quantum phenomena do not establish uncaused beginnings or defeat a causal explanation.
moves.lockedProposition: Quantum mechanics has deterministic interpretations, vacuum fluctuations are not from nothing, and even zero energy still requires a cause.

Live burden: The reply must connect the possibility of deterministic causes and the claim that particles emerge from something to a positive causal requirement for zero-energy cosmological origins.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
moves.currentDescription: Quantum decays and atomic transitions undermine universal causation, while cosmologies permitting an earlier universe challenge a necessary temporal beginning and its personal-creator inference.
moves.lockedProposition: Quantum events challenge universal causation, while published cosmologies allow an earlier universe and do not require time to begin.

Live burden: He must establish that the cited processes lack causes under an interpretation and that beginningless cosmologies remain physically credible enough to block the inference from a temporal beginning to a personal creator.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues causation need not be temporally prior: as a ceiling simultaneously supports a chandelier, God may cause the universe at its first moment while becoming temporal.
moves.lockedProposition: Causation need not precede its effect; creation can be simultaneous with the universe’s first moment as God becomes temporal.

Live burden: Craig must justify extending this familiar physical relation beyond time and explain how divine agency supplies genuine origination rather than coexistence at the temporal boundary.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
moves.currentDescription: Published no-boundary and tunneling models permit natural transitions from prior chaos or universes, so a beginning and external cause remain unestablished despite Craig’s boundary argument.

Live burden: Stenger must substantiate how the models describe natural transitions, distinguish permitting beginningless history from demonstrating it, and explain why a prior universe or chaos avoids rather than relocates Craig’s causal demand.

moves.sectionTitle: Naturalistic Explanatory Reach: Design, Mind, and Time
moves.currentDescription: Eternal vacuum fluctuations should produce coalesced, infinitely old universes contrary to observation, supporting a past boundary for expanding cosmologies against natural quantum-origin accounts.
moves.lockedProposition: An eternal vacuum would yield observational consequences not seen, while expanding cosmologies require a past spacetime boundary.

Live burden: Craig must connect those models' failure to expanding cosmologies generally and exclude finite, revised, or nonvacuum natural accounts before treating boundary dependence as explanatory support for God.

moves.sectionTitle: Naturalistic Explanatory Reach: Design, Mind, and Time
moves.currentDescription: Brain injury, chemicals, illness, and anesthesia disrupt consciousness, while scans map thoughts and emotions to neuronal firing, supporting natural brain dependence over an immaterial immortal soul.
moves.lockedProposition: Consciousness varies with physical brain conditions, and neuroscience increasingly models thoughts and emotions naturally.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The move links brain injury, chemicals, illness, and anesthesia causing unconsciousness with precise scans associating thoughts and emotions with neuronal firing, then cites laboratory testing of brain-produced consciousness models. Principal limitation: Dependence and correlation favor natural explanation, but neither proves every conscious feature is brain-produced nor excludes an immaterial soul operating through physical conditions, leaving evidence warrant and calibration weaker. Live burden: It must show why physical modulation and testable models establish production rather than dependence alone and thereby preclude consciousness continuing after death.

moves.sectionTitle: Naturalistic Explanatory Reach: Design, Mind, and Time
moves.currentDescription: Human brain dependence does not exclude an unembodied God, because jubilation and sadness are mental rather than neural properties, leaving materialism to explain identity and agency.
moves.lockedProposition: Human mind-brain dependence does not disprove an unembodied God, and mental properties, identity, intentionality, and agency resist reduction.

Live burden: The pro side must justify the bridge from mental properties to an immaterial person, showing why competing material accounts cannot preserve identity and causal agency over time.

moves.sectionTitle: Naturalistic Explanatory Reach: Design, Mind, and Time
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues logical conclusions inherit their premises’ weakness, whereas physical reasons permit complexity from simpler states, challenging theistic coherence and cumulative evidence to establish divine necessity.
moves.lockedProposition: Logic is only as sound as its premises, while physical processes give reason to model complexity arising naturally from simpler states.

Live burden: The reply must identify which theistic premises fail and develop the physical account enough to show natural emergence undercuts divine necessity, not merely offers another possibility.

moves.sectionTitle: Naturalistic Explanatory Reach: Design, Mind, and Time
moves.currentDescription: Because materialism makes beliefs products of physical determination and survival selection, Craig argues it cannot warrant its own truth, challenging brain-dependence and current-data claims.
moves.lockedProposition: If beliefs are determined by matter and selected merely for survival, materialism undercuts warrant for its own truth.

Live burden: Craig must show reliable cognition would not aid survival, distinguish causal origins from epistemic justification, and answer the strongest materialist truth-tracking account before defeating either targeted claim.

moves.sectionTitle: Naturalistic Explanatory Reach: Design, Mind, and Time
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues time is a human-built concept in physical models, so Craig cannot assume mind-independent time when describing simultaneous timeless causation without further justification.
moves.lockedProposition: Treating time as a mind-independent entity is unwarranted because physical time is a modeling concept for observations.

Live burden: Stenger must explain why time’s role as a modeling concept precludes its corresponding to reality, then show how that conclusion defeats Craig’s causation account rather than redescribing physicists’ practice.

moves.sectionTitle: Naturalistic Explanatory Reach: Design, Mind, and Time
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues that present data remain compatible with a wholly material universe, while openness to future spiritual evidence makes irreducible-mind claims bear an evidentiary burden.

Live burden: He must show how materialism explains those mental properties, or provide evidence undermining their alleged irreducibility, rather than rely on the absence of accepted spiritual evidence.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, Hiddenness, and the Evidential Force of Evil

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, Hiddenness, and the Evidential Force of Evil
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues philosophers abandoned strict incompatibility because atheists must exclude morally sufficient reasons, but must still show why suffering does not make Christianity improbable.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, Hiddenness, and the Evidential Force of Evil
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues that pervasive misery fits an evil deity better than a good one, challenging divine-grounding accounts to reconcile objective morality with suffering.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Stenger directly contrasts pervasive worldly misery with divine goodness, arguing that observed suffering fits an evil deity better, which makes the objection especially responsive and logically intelligible. Principal limitation: The excerpt offers no substantiation beyond suffering’s asserted prevalence, and evil-deity compatibility neither demonstrates inconsistency between misery and unidentified divine intentions nor addresses morality’s claimed objective, nonintersubjective divine grounding. Live burden: Stenger must connect suffering specifically to the morality arguments by establishing that their divine foundation entails benevolence and cannot accommodate apparently gratuitous misery.

moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Warrant
moves.currentDescription: The disciples embraced resurrection despite Jewish expectations against a dying Messiah or pre-end-time glorification, so their transformed conviction supports divine action over naturalistic explanations.

Live burden: Pro must substantiate those premises, compare specific natural explanations with resurrection, and show why costly commitment indicates truth rather than sincerity alone.

moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Warrant

Principal limitation: Its evidentiary warrant remains weak because the excerpt asserts Roman historical silence and scholarly rejection without developing source dates, the scholars' arguments, or why Paul's omission undermines accounts. Live burden: It must establish that these silences and disputes substantially reduce the empty tomb's probability to defeat the resurrection inference, while addressing whether Gospel testimony or alternative evidence can sustain that premise.

moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Warrant

Live burden: The reply must demonstrate that independent streams substantiate the disputed resurrection facts, justify relying on four biographies, and connect those facts specifically to divine action rather than existence or crucifixion alone.

moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Warrant

moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Warrant
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues the empty tomb surfaces only decades later, is absent from Paul, and faces contradictions, so an empty tomb cannot uniquely establish resurrection.

moves.sectionTitle: Public Evidence, Revelation, and Prayer
moves.currentDescription: God’s existence need not produce public evidence because immediate knowledge or selective revelation to willing responders would undercut arguments from absent evidence and hiddenness.

Live burden: The reply must justify why a loving God would prefer immediate or selective disclosure, identify who counts as willing, and explain sincere nonbelievers without merely assuming their resistance.

moves.sectionTitle: Public Evidence, Revelation, and Prayer
moves.currentDescription: For an interventionist Abrahamic God, missing observations are evidence against existence when that God predicts detectable effects, shifting the burden toward explaining their absence.

moves.sectionTitle: Public Evidence, Revelation, and Prayer
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues Stenger left both expected-evidence premises unsupported, whereas origins, morality, and resurrection provide objective evidence, shifting the closing comparison toward theism.

Live burden: Craig must substantiate how each cited domain objectively supports God and show why Stenger’s probability premises fail, while still meeting the extraordinary-claim demand and the verification challenge to inner experience.

moves.sectionTitle: Public Evidence, Revelation, and Prayer
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues that erroneous scriptural teachings and the absence of verified modern revelations undermine claims that divine communication supplies inaccessible knowledge or reliable predictions.

Live burden: Con must substantiate the absence across modern revelations and predictions, while showing why scriptural errors defeat divine communication rather than only interpretations, authors, or traditions.

moves.sectionTitle: Public Evidence, Revelation, and Prayer
moves.currentDescription: Controlled studies at Harvard, Duke, and Mayo found no significant health benefit from intercessory prayer, weakening prayer’s proposed role as scientifically confirmable divine action.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The move cites controlled health studies at Harvard, Duke, and Mayo, then reasonably infers that null intercessory prayer results weaken prayer as scientifically confirmable divine action. Live burden: The argument must explain why a deity should produce measurable health benefits under these protocols, what effects remain expected despite unanswered prayers, and why repeated null findings implicate God rather than intercessory efficacy.

moves.sectionTitle: Personal Experience and Competing Proof Burdens
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues people can know God directly through personal experience, as biblical believers encountered an active will, making experiential knowledge support the cumulative theistic case.
moves.lockedProposition: People can know God immediately through personal experience, and the cumulative six-part case favors theism.

Principal limitation: The excerpt describes what such encounters felt like but supplies no experience-independent corroborative basis for identifying their object as God, leaving evidence warrant notably weaker than its clarity and responsiveness. Live burden: The pro side must show why these experiences reliably disclose God rather than merely producing conviction, and how this experiential premise adds probative weight to the cumulative six-part case.

moves.sectionTitle: Personal Experience and Competing Proof Burdens

moves.sectionTitle: Personal Experience and Competing Proof Burdens
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues Craig’s supernatural being is the more extravagant claim, so it bears a heavier burden than explaining origins and complexity through plausible natural scenarios.
moves.lockedProposition: The more extraordinary supernatural claim bears the heavier burden; plausible natural origin and complexity scenarios suffice for Stenger’s alternative.

moves.sectionTitle: Personal Experience and Competing Proof Burdens
moves.currentDescription: Stenger argues sincere inner experiences remain compatible with mental origins unless they yield otherwise unknowable information, challenging personal experience as proof of external revelation.
moves.lockedProposition: Inner experiences need independently unavailable information to distinguish external revelation from events wholly within a person’s mind.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: um I don't not have to deny also that many people have what they sincerely believe is is an inner experience of God all I have to do is argue that this in inner experience can all be in their heads uh the way to prove that the inner experience is legitimate and not just something in their heads would be again for someone to come back with some knowledge that they could not possibly have known no one has ever done that just like my argument against Revelation uh and I think those arguments that I made early in the uh in the talk have not been rebutted
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Stenger concedes sincerity yet offers an independently testable discriminator, otherwise unknowable information, which separates external revelation from wholly intrapersonal experience and directly answers experiential proof claims. Principal limitation: The claim that nobody has produced such knowledge receives no examples or substantiation, while this exceptionally demanding criterion may disregard alternative indicators, making evidential warrant substantially weaker than logical coherence. Live burden: Proponents of cumulative personal experience and immediate selective knowledge must explain how inner experience evidences an external God without independently unavailable information, or supply comparably discriminating verification.
